points: Publish-subscribe lets a producer announce that something happened without knowing who needs to hear it: every subscription gets its own copy of each message.
A queue hands each message to one consumer; pub-sub hands it to every subscription, and only inside a subscription do consumers share the work.
Spotify gives each kind of message its own topic and pipeline, so a noisy or blocked kind delays only itself.
Uber's Consumer Proxy gives up order inside a partition so any worker can take any message, which suits only work where order does not matter.

figures.label: over 8 million events per second global peak at the end of Q1 2019
over 300 microservices use Kafka for pub-sub message queueing

prerequisiteReasons.message-queues: Publish-subscribe takes from message queues the lease, the acknowledgement and at-least-once delivery, now applied to each subscription separately.

points: Rate limiting caps how many requests a client can make in a window of time, so one noisy caller cannot use up shared capacity.
Counting is easy on one machine and hard across many, so real systems trade a little accuracy for speed and keep the shared count off the request path.
Cloudflare chooses the counting algorithm by what its store can do atomically and cheaply, and keeps the block decision as a small flag servers can cache.
Databricks counts locally, reports in batches and lets each key's owner answer with a time to reject until, accepting some overshoot.

figures.label: 0.003% of requests wrongly allowed or limited in the accuracy test
tail latency improvement of up to 10x in some cases

prerequisiteReasons.caching: Rate limiting takes from caching the idea of keeping a small piece of state close to the request, and of tolerating a slightly stale copy.
prerequisiteReasons.consistent-hashing: Rate limiting takes from consistent hashing the way to send every request for one key to the same owner of its counter.

points: Replication keeps copies of a database on several machines so reads can spread out and a failed primary can be replaced.
The hard questions are when a write counts as safe, and how to pick and announce a new primary without two machines accepting writes at once.
Meta put promotions and membership changes into the replication log, which removes a whole class of coordination bugs.
GitHub gives each part one job, decides by quorum across data centers, and never depends on the failed node to help.

figures.label: typical failover about 2 s with Raft, 20 to 40 s with semi-synchronous replication
typical planned promotion takes about 300 ms

prerequisiteReasons.databases: Replication takes from databases the write-ahead log, since replicas stay current by replaying the primary's log in the same order.

points: Sharding splits one large dataset across many databases by a key, so each database stores and serves only part of it.
The key decides which queries stay on one shard and which must visit all of them, and the layout decides how hard adding machines later is.
Figma gives each shard a fixed range of hashed keys instead of a hash ring, and splits the move into a logical step and a physical one.
Notion fixes the number of shards and grows by moving whole shards between hosts, choosing a shard count with many divisors.

figures.label: almost 100x growth of Figma's database stack since 2020
32 physical databases at launch, 15 shards each

prerequisiteReasons.replication: Sharding takes from replication the idea of data spread over several machines, and the question of which machine holds which data.
prerequisiteReasons.consistent-hashing: Sharding takes from consistent hashing the idea of mapping a key to a machine, and the contrast with a fixed range of hashed keys per shard.
